design_detail: Narrative review (journal section: Review), presented as part of the Canadian Association of Poison Control Centres symposium at the North American Congress of Clinical Toxicology, October 2000 (p. 47), on interpreting drug concentrations measured after death: redistribution and differences between sampling sites, whole blood against serum, alternative specimens (vitreous humour, skeletal muscle, bile, adipose tissue, organs), production and loss of analytes after death, false-positive immunoassays after haemolysis, embalming and storage, ending with nine questions for the toxicologist. Nine tables list drugs in which redistribution probably does not occur (20 entries), approximate heart-to-peripheral blood (C:P) ratios for about 100 drugs, recommended tissues for some poisonings, bile and blood concentration pairs, single post-mortem blood levels for five psychotropic drugs, analytes open to false-positive urine immunoassay, autopsy findings linked to toxins, embalming effects and storage problems. No search method, selection criteria or appraisal; 90 references from 1975 to 2002.
can_establish: Which factors a physician toxicologist and a poison-centre pharmacist considered necessary in 2003 for interpreting a drug concentration measured after death, the checklist they proposed, and pointers to the literature on each factor.
cannot_establish: The size or frequency of any effect described (ratios and thresholds come without case numbers, ranges or per-drug sources), whether the literature was selected completely or fairly, or how reliable any listed fatal level or heart-to-peripheral ratio is for a given death.

sample.inclusion_exclusion: No search or criteria stated; 90 references (1975–2002) chosen by the authors: case reports and series, animal studies, analytical-method papers, reviews and textbooks.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence selection is the authors'. By the titles of the works cited, several statements rest on animal or single-case evidence: the timing of morphine redistribution on two rat studies and one human study (refs 5–7), diffusion from the stomach into the liver on a rat model (ref. 16, which the text labels as an animal model), and the vitreous-to-blood ethanol range on a dog study of fluoxetine and one road-death case (refs 36 and 53). The heart-to-peripheral ratios are cited collectively (refs 14, 15 and 20–33) without saying which source, or how many cases, gave each value.

exposure.polysubstance: Co-ingested drugs are named as one reason deaths from newer antidepressants and antipsychotics are hard to recognize (p. 50); not otherwise addressed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (review). The review stresses comparison with a blood sample taken just before or at death and between several post-mortem sampling sites (p. 48).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The review lists tolerance and dosing interval among the clinical information needed to interpret a level (p. 52, question 4) but offers no way to establish tolerance after death.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratios (Table 2, p. 49), tissue concentration thresholds (Table 3, p. 50), bile and blood concentration pairs (Table 4, p. 51), single post-mortem blood levels presented as associated with psychotropic deaths (Table 5, p. 51), analytes open to false-positive immunoassay (Table 6, p. 51).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validity data; the tabulated values come without case numbers, ranges (except cocaine and imipramine in Table 2) or per-drug sources.
outcomes.operationalization: Potential for redistribution is equated with a high heart-to-peripheral ratio (p. 48), and drugs with an apparent volume of distribution above 3 L/kg are called candidates for redistribution (p. 50, no source cited).

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, without sources per value. Heart-to-peripheral ratios (Table 2, p. 49): amphetamine 2.0, methamphetamine 2.4 (listed separately as D-methamphetamine 2.1), MDMA 2.65, MBDB 2.5, paramethoxyamphetamine 1.6, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3, morphine (heroin) 2.2, codeine 1.8, oxycodone 3.1, pethidine 2.1, ketamine 1.6, phencyclidine 1.8, gamma-hydroxybutyrate 2, diazepam 1.6, alprazolam 1.5, flunitrazepam 3, midazolam 4, doxepin 5.5, strychnine 15, hydrochlorothiazide 23; alfentanil, methylfentanyl, remifentanil, sufentanil and tetrahydrocannabinol are listed without a ratio. Whole blood against serum: 12–18% for ethanol and a factor of 1.6 for cannabinoids; vitreous humour ethanol 0.9–1.3 times blood; ethanol produced by putrefaction usually about 0.05 g%, developing over 3–10 days (p. 50).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The tables give single values without the spread or number of cases behind them. A cited study whose title reports a lack of predictable site-dependent differences for cocaine, benzoylecgonine and cocaethylene (ref. 23, p. 54) is not discussed, while Table 2 gives cocaine a ratio of 1.5 to 2.3 (p. 49).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A catalogue, drawn from cited literature, of reasons a drug concentration measured after death may not reflect the concentration at death: redistribution (heart blood higher than peripheral blood for many basic drugs), whole blood against serum, production or loss of analyte after death, false-positive immunoassays after haemolysis, embalming and storage; with tabulated ratios, thresholds and levels whose evidence base is not shown.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion is cautious: extrapolating an autopsy result to the state before death may not always be possible, and limited knowledge of change after death can lead to incorrect assumptions (pp. 52–53). Within the text, certainty is sometimes raised beyond what is shown: the drugs of Table 1 are said to have been demonstrated not to change (p. 47) while the table's own title says redistribution probably does not occur (p. 48); Table 5 gives single blood levels said to be directly associated with psychotropic deaths (p. 50), without site, number of cases, spread or co-ingestants, which sits uneasily with the review's own message; and the volume-of-distribution threshold and the statement that cocaethylene would not be formed after death are given without a source (p. 50). For one drug the listed level falls below a typical post-mortem value: olanzapine 0.160 mg/L here (p. 51), while Ketola & Kriikku (2019) list a median femoral-blood concentration of 0.2 mg/L regardless of cause of death (their Table 1, PDF p. 41; editors' cross-check).

timeline.event: Pounder & Jones, four-case series showing several-fold differences in drug concentrations between blood sampled from different vessels after death (read in this batch); this review cites Pounder's 1993 book chapter instead.

Ketola & Kriikku compile paired within-case ratios with numbers of results; their median ratios of other blood (such as cardiac blood) to femoral blood are lower than this review's single heart-to-peripheral values for several of the same drugs (morphine 1.26 against 2.2, methamphetamine 1.50 against 2.4, oxycodone 1.19 against 3.1, diazepam 0.95 against 1.6).
Borra et al., a review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: The factors the review lists remain the frame used for interpreting post-mortem toxicology. Its single-value heart-to-peripheral ratios can now be checked against compilations that give numbers of results (Ketola & Kriikku 2019, read in this batch), which show lower typical central-to-femoral ratios for several of the same drugs and wide variation between drugs.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Leikin: Evanston Northwestern Healthcare OMEGA, Glenbrook Hospital, Glenview, Illinois; Watson: South Texas Poison Center, Department of Surgery, University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio (p. 47). Five of the 90 references are the authors' own (refs 4, 9, 27, 35 and 83). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with an explicit search and appraisal of studies that measured the same drug in blood at or just before death and at several post-mortem sites, reporting for each drug the number of cases and the spread of ratios; and, for tables of fatal levels, studies comparing concentrations in deaths attributed to a drug with deaths from other causes in which the same drug was present, by sampling site.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence.
No appraisal; animal, single-case and human series evidence are mixed without labels in places (morphine timing; vitreous ethanol range), and tabulated values carry no case numbers.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Five of 90 references are the authors' own; the central points rest on others' work.

Uncited generalizations (volume of distribution above 3 L/kg; cocaethylene not formed after death), Table 1 described in the text as demonstrated although its title says probably, and single fatal levels presented as direct associations; the conclusion itself is cautious.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how predictable site differences are
domains.note: Single heart-to-peripheral values per drug are offered as guides; evidence of between-case variation and unpredictability is under-represented (a cited cocaine study titled as finding no predictable site differences is not discussed).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, and the overall judgment can be no milder than the worst domain. The review is a clear practitioner's guide with a cautious conclusion, but its selection is unsystematic and its tables give single numbers without sources or spread. Citable for: the list of factors that can make a post-mortem concentration differ from the concentration at death (sampling site and redistribution, whole blood against serum, production or loss after death, false-positive immunoassays after haemolysis, embalming, storage) and the authors' nine-question checklist, as the authors' expert view. Not citable for: any specific heart-to-peripheral ratio, tissue threshold or fatal level as an established value; claims resting on it alone stay at draft and say their figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Comparing a post-mortem concentration with therapeutic and toxic ranges from the living assumes the concentration does not change during and after death; the authors call this assumption incorrect for many substances and say post-mortem change must be considered for all but a few drugs, listed in Table 1 (20 entries, including alcohols, carbon monoxide, carbamazepine, hydrocodone, lorazepam, mirtazapine and zopiclone) under the title of drugs in which redistribution probably does not occur.
key_findings.locator: 1st paragraph (p. 47, left column continuing in right column); Table 1 (p. 48)

key_findings.finding: Interpretation ideally rests on a consistent relationship between the concentration at a specific site at death (usually venous plasma or serum) and the post-mortem concentration; dose, time of intake before death, route, tolerance and whether steady state was reached all affect the concentration–effect relationship, and most such relationships come from trough levels at steady state during therapy.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph, beginning 'The goal of interpreting' (p. 47, right column, continuing on p. 48, left column)

key_findings.finding: Redistribution can be fast: thiopental and pentobarbital concentrations rose significantly in the first 4 hours after death (ref. 4); morphine rose within the first few minutes when compared with samples from before or around death, but no rise was seen when the first sample was taken 3 hours or more after death (refs 5–7). Because the rate of redistribution is generally unknown, post-mortem samples should be compared with one taken immediately before or at death, and from multiple sites.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'To expand our understanding' (left column, continuing at the top of the right column)
key_findings.note: By their titles (p. 53), refs 5 and 7 are studies in rats and ref. 6 a study in humans; the text does not say so.

key_findings.finding: Proposed mechanisms: passive diffusion along concentration gradients as tissue breaks down, with fluid shifts, pH, volume of distribution and the body's condition; stomach, liver, bladder and lungs as sources; gravity-dependent blood flow; in supine bodies, rapid diffusion of basic drugs from the lungs into the left heart chambers; and diffusion from the myocardium into heart blood, which the authors call debatable. Ethanol from the stomach can contaminate pericardial blood, but only after large amounts (400 ml of 10% ethanol), with minimal contamination of femoral vein samples (ref. 18).
key_findings.locator: Paragraphs beginning 'The assumption that death results' and 'Recent studies have demonstrated' (right column)

key_findings.finding: Heart-to-peripheral blood ratios are offered as a measure of the potential for redistribution, with high ratios meaning heart or pericardial samples may overstate concentrations. Table 2 lists about 100 drugs, for example amphetamine 2.0, methamphetamine 2.4 (D-methamphetamine 2.1), MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3, morphine (heroin) 2.2, codeine 1.8, oxycodone 3.1, ketamine 1.6, phencyclidine 1.8, gamma-hydroxybutyrate 2, diazepam 1.6, alprazolam 1.5, midazolam 4, doxepin 5.5; tetrahydrocannabinol and several fentanyl analogues are listed without a ratio.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The cardiac to peripheral blood level' (p. 48, right column); Table 2 (p. 49)
key_findings.note: No case numbers, ranges (except cocaine and imipramine) or per-drug sources; the table is cited collectively to refs 14, 15 and 20–33 (p. 50).

key_findings.finding: Whole blood, the usual post-mortem matrix, differs from the serum or plasma used clinically: by 12–18% for ethanol and by a factor of 1.6 for cannabinoids (refs 34, 35); clotting, fluid movement and cellular changes after death alter the blood sampled.

Drugs with an apparent volume of distribution above 3 L/kg are called candidates for redistribution (no source given); transformation of parent drug to metabolites after death is described as rare (nitrobenzodiazepines); ethanol produced by putrefaction in decomposed bodies is usually about 0.05 g% and takes 3 to 10 days to develop; and cocaethylene is said not to be expected to form after death by this mechanism (no source given).
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'An analysis of the drugs' (left column)

key_findings.finding: Alternative specimens: skeletal muscle (especially the lateral dome of the diaphragm) as a stable matrix for qualitative detection; bile for identifying drugs concentrated in the liver; drugs in adipose tissue reflecting distribution before death; vitreous humour often the only other matrix allowing quantitative interpretation, with vitreous ethanol 0.9 to 1.3 times blood and lagging behind it, and vitreous useful for 6-acetylmorphine, benzodiazepines and electrolytes.
key_findings.locator: Paragraphs beginning 'Alternative matrices' and 'The vitreous humor' (left column, the second continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Recommended tissues (Table 3) include brain or cerebellum for heroin, with a cerebellum-to-blood morphine ratio of about 1 when death occurs within 1 hour of administration and 3.5 when it occurs within 2 to 48 hours, and 6-acetylmorphine in cerebrospinal fluid detecting 46% more heroin-related cases than blood; fentanyl liver concentrations over 69 µg/kg associated with overdose; vitreous potassium to estimate the post-mortem interval (hours = 7.14 × potassium − 39.1); lidocaine kidney-to-liver ratio below 1 after absorption from the trachea during intubation and above 1 after intravenous treatment.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and its footnotes a and b (right column)

key_findings.finding: About 3% of all deaths are listed by medical examiners as of unknown cause, and up to 10% of sudden deaths among people with long-term heavy drinking may be of unknown cause; a blood beta-hydroxybutyrate level over 2500 µmol/L may indicate alcoholic ketoacidosis as the cause of death (ref. 56).
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Another example of postmortem blood results' (right column)

key_findings.finding: Table 5 lists single post-mortem blood levels that the authors present as directly associated with psychotropic-related deaths: fluoxetine 0.63, paroxetine 0.4, sertraline 1.5, olanzapine 0.160 and trazodone 9 mg/L (refs 57–59).
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Death due to newer antidepressant' (p. 50, right column); Table 5 (p. 51)
key_findings.note: Single values without sampling site, number of cases, spread or co-ingestants.

key_findings.finding: Haemolysis after death can raise lactate dehydrogenase, lactic acid and protein in serum and urine, which can make urine immunoassays falsely positive for amphetamines, barbiturates, opiates, cocaine metabolite, propoxyphene and benzodiazepines (Table 6; refs 60, 61); C-reactive protein appears not to change after death (ref. 62).
key_findings.locator: Table 6 (p. 51); paragraph beginning 'Due to postmortem hemolysis' (p. 52, left column)
key_findings.note: How often this happens and with which assays is not stated; ref. 61 concerns the EMIT drugs-of-abuse assay, by its title (p. 55).

key_findings.finding: Nine questions the toxicologist must address before judging a drug's role in a death: whether several sites were sampled and where; whether the drug is known or suspected to redistribute; whether data define the concentration–toxicity relationship; whether clinical information on the exposure (for example tolerance, dosing interval) is adequate; whether the concentration was clinically sufficient to cause, prevent or be directly involved in the death; whether autopsy findings typical of the overdose exist; whether the body was embalmed; whether the analyte needs special storage; and whether pills in the stomach contain active drug or are drug-free wax matrices.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Thus, it is clear' and questions 1–9 (left and right columns)

key_findings.finding: Embalming (Table 8) may raise amitriptyline and lower nortriptyline (65% conversion in 24 h), slightly lower liver fentanyl, reduce blood ethanol and benzodiazepines and raise methanol, with no apparent effect on morphine; formaldehyde at 5 to 20% methylates tricyclic amines. Storage (Table 9): 6-acetylmorphine is stable at −20 °C; morphine and its metabolites degrade at 4 °C but not at −20 °C; gamma-hydroxybutyrate may be artificially raised in citrate-buffered blood; LSD needs protection from light and heat.

Conclusion: even when a concentration is available from an autopsy sample, interpreting it and extrapolating it to the state before death may not always be possible; the drug's post-mortem stability and potential for redistribution must be built into the interpretation, and further animal research and multiple-site, timely ante-mortem and post-mortem measurements are needed.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion (p. 52, right column, continuing on p. 53)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says post-mortem changes have been demonstrated not to occur for the drugs of Table 1, while the table's title says redistribution probably does not occur in them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 should be cited as the authors' judgment that redistribution is probably absent, not as demonstrated.

reporting_issues.issue: In one sentence, putrefactive ethanol is usually in the range of 0.05 gm%, although concentrations of up to 0.2 mg% are infrequently found; the second unit makes the upper value lower than the usual one.
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper value is probably 0.2 g%; as printed (0.2 mg%, 250 times lower than 0.05 g%; editors' calculation) it cannot be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4's title gives a bile-to-blood ratio in mg/L, but its entries are pairs of concentrations (for example heroin (morphine) 32–0.43, cocaine 0.7–0.2); colchicine appears twice with different blood values (2.9–0.6 as Cochicine, 2.9–0.06 as Colchicine). Table 2 lists venlafaxine twice and methamphetamine and D-methamphetamine with different ratios (2.4, 2.1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 4 entries are best read as single example concentration pairs without source or case number, not as ratios; the duplicates suggest the tables were not checked closely.

reporting_issues.issue: References 52 (adipose tissue) and 62 (C-reactive protein) are two different papers printed with the same citation, Forensic Sci Int 2001;121:157–160.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two supporting statements cannot be traced as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that limited knowledge of post-mortem change can lead to incorrect assumptions cites ref. 81 (in vitro production of gamma-hydroxybutyrate in urine samples), while ref. 83 (Watson & McKinney, on the practical interpretation of post-mortem concentrations) is listed but never cited in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; probably a numbering slip, with the statement meant to cite ref. 83, by the second author.

reporting_issues.issue: The vitreous-to-blood ethanol range of 0.9 to 1.3 is cited to refs 36 and 53, which by their titles are a study of fluoxetine and norfluoxetine in dogs and a single road-death case.
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be traced to a study comparing vitreous and blood ethanol across many cases; it needs a primary source before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives cocaine a heart-to-peripheral ratio of 1.5 to 2.3, while ref. 23, cited among the sources for site differences, is titled as reporting a lack of predictable site-dependent and time-dependent differences for cocaine, benzoylecgonine and cocaethylene; the text does not discuss it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cocaine ratio, and single ratios generally, may suggest more predictability than the cited evidence supports.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), pp. 47–56 (all pages, Tables 1–9 and the reference list read and checked on rendered pages, where the text layer misprints some symbols, for example µmol/L as mmol/L and > as a full stop; no supplement)
